To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sustained demand for education in less developed countries is rational and can be understood in terms of the following three propositions: First, the private benefits of education are positively related to the level of education.

in less-developed countries the private demand for education will be sustained even if the supply is in excess of demand, and the demand will be sustained even when the educated individual faces a substantial surplus of similar individuals in the labor market.

the demand for higher education in less-developed countries is likely to be high and to persist in the long-run, even in the face of a substantial excess supply of educated labor, because of (1) the positive impact of education on earnings, (2) the positive impact on earnings of the ability to obtain a job, and (3) the positive impact that education has on the probability of finding a job in the first place.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: Why is there a high and sustained demand for education in a country with a surplus of educated labor?

in the presence of a large surplus of educated labor, the private demand for education will be sustained, even in the absence of government intervention, because the net benefits of education are positive.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, given the labor market conditions which are likely to be prevalent in the less developed countries, the private demand for education will be sustained.

the private demand for education in less developed countries is likely to remain high even if there is a surplus of educated labor in the economy, and this demand is likely to be sustained for a considerable period of time.
the private demand for education can be explained by a combination of the private benefits from the educated individual in the labor market and the public benefits of a more educated labor force.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a sustained demand for education in a country with a substantial surplus of labor does not necessarily imply that the labor market is not functioning efficiently.
the demand for schooling is not necessarily a function of the supply of schooling.
the private demand for education can persist for a long time in the presence of a surplus of educated labor and a large number of unemployed educated individuals.
